In a maneuver they nicknamed the "Big Bang," engineers simultaneously powered down certain components on the spacecraft and swapped in lower-energy alternatives, all while keeping the craft's aging systems within the narrow thermal range they need to survive the cold of interstellar space. The result was roughly an extra year of operating power squeezed out of a spacecraft that already has almost nothing left to spare.

Voyager 2 now runs on just three of its original ten scientific instruments, after two were switched off back in 2024 on each of the twin Voyager probes to conserve power. Every watt matters at this point, which is what made project manager Suzanne Dodd's description of the trade-offs so pointed: "Every watt saved now is a decision about what data humanity still gets to learn from out there." It's a stark way of putting it, but an accurate one. Every instrument still running on Voyager 2 is actively returning data from a region of space no other spacecraft has ever reached, so keeping one more sensor alive for one more year is keeping open a window onto interstellar space that, once closed, closes for good.

NASA now plans to apply the same power-saving modifications to Voyager 1 in the coming months, extending the trick to both of the aging twins launched back in 1977. Neither spacecraft can be repaired or serviced, obviously, so every gain in operating life comes purely from clever engineering done from a distance of more than fifteen billion miles.

It's a modest-sounding fix, a bit of rewiring and a new nickname, but the stakes are anything but small. Voyager 2 remains the only object humanity has ever built to keep functioning and communicating from beyond the influence of our sun, and this quiet bit of ingenuity means it will keep doing that for at least another year.

stories.headline: Restored California Creek Helps Threatened Salmon Grow Twice as Fast and Doubles Their Survival
stories.summary: A restoration project turned a former lumber mill site on Prairie Creek, California, into wetlands and side channels where young coho salmon can rest and feed before reaching the ocean. Fish there grew up to twice as fast as those in the unrestored creek, and 2.6% of the 2023 cohort returned as adults to spawn, more than double the roughly 1% survival rate seen before.
stories.narrative:
Along California's redwood coast, a stretch of water called Prairie Creek has become one of the last refuges for three struggling salmon species: California Coastal Chinook, Northern California steelhead, and coho salmon, whose numbers have fallen by 90 percent over the past century. For decades the creek ran through the site of a former lumber mill, its natural floodplain cut off and its side channels filled in, leaving young fish with little food and few places to hide from predators or fast-moving water.

NOAA Fisheries and its partners set out to undo that damage, reconnecting the creek to its floodplain and rebuilding the wetlands, ponds, and slow-moving side channels that juvenile salmon depend on in their first months of life. The idea is simple: give young fish calmer water and more food, and they will grow bigger and stronger before they ever have to face the ocean.

The early results have exceeded what biologists expected. Carter Adamson, a fish biologist with the Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission, found that in some sites and some years, juvenile coho using the restored habitat grew up to twice as fast as fish in the main creek. That extra size matters enormously, because bigger, stronger smolts are far more likely to survive the perilous transition to saltwater and the years they spend at sea.

The numbers bear that out. Among the coho salmon that hatched in 2023, 2.6 percent survived their time in the Pacific and returned to Prairie Creek as adults to spawn, more than double the roughly 1 percent survival rate researchers had documented before the restoration. For a species that has lost the vast majority of its historic population, that kind of gain is a meaningful step back from the brink.

Researchers with Cal Poly Humboldt and NOAA Fisheries plan to keep monitoring the creek through 2028 to see whether the gains hold up over time. But the early data offers a hopeful blueprint for other watersheds trying to bring depleted salmon runs back: sometimes the most effective fix isn't a hatchery or a fishing restriction, but simply giving a river back the slow water and hiding places it always used to have.

stories.headline: Once-Distrustful Rescue Horse Learns to 'Play' Guitar and Harp, Earning a Spot on a Debut Album
stories.summary: Yupia, a rescued horse with a troubled past at a Moorpark, California rescue facility, spent nine months distrusting people until singer-songwriter Mikayla Khramov began playing guitar near his pasture. He started nosing the strings to change the chords, and his sounds will now feature on two songs of her upcoming debut album.
stories.narrative:
When Mikayla Khramov started volunteering at a horse rescue in Moorpark, California, she met a seven-year-old Kentucky-bred horse named Yupia who wanted nothing to do with people. He had come to the rescue with behavioral issues and a deep-seated distrust that nine months of gentle, patient volunteering had barely begun to soften.

Khramov, a Los Angeles singer-songwriter, didn't try to win him over with treats or formal training exercises. Instead, one day she simply brought her guitar out to the pasture and started playing. What happened next surprised her: Yupia wandered over on his own, and instead of shying away, he began moving his mouth and snout across the strings, changing the chords as he went.

It kept happening. Whatever instrument she brought out, Yupia would approach and start experimenting with it, first strumming clumsily with his nose and, over time, working out how to press the strings with his teeth. When Khramov introduced her harp, he responded the same way, treating it like just another instrument to explore rather than something to fear.

For Khramov, the connection ran both directions. She has said the horse helped her fall back in love with music at a point when it had started to feel like a job rather than a passion. Rather than sessions that felt like obligations, her time with Yupia became something closer to play, a reminder of why she wanted to make music in the first place.

That partnership is now headed for a wider audience. Khramov is folding the sounds Yupia makes into two songs on her upcoming debut album, which blends Portuguese musicians with folk and electronic influences and is due out in September. What began as one horse slowly learning to trust a person with a guitar has turned into an unlikely creative collaboration, credited on the record for the part he played in making it.

stories.headline: Stress Hormone Discovered to Help the Brain Repair Itself After Injury
stories.summary: Researchers found that after brain injury, cells called oligodendrocyte progenitor cells release the stress hormone CRH near the damaged area, which helps guide those cells to mature and rebuild myelin, the protective insulation around nerve fibers. The discovery reveals a natural repair pathway and could point toward new treatments for brain damage.

stories.headline: Rescued Orangutans Released Into the Wild Are Now Raising Babies of Their Own
stories.summary: Nearly 200 rescued and rehabilitated Sumatran orangutans released into Indonesia's Jantho Pine Forest Nature Reserve over the past 15 years have successfully adapted to the wild, and at least 10 babies have now been born there. The births mark the establishment of an entirely new wild population of the critically endangered species.

stories.headline: Chester Zoo Hatches Five Secretarybird Chicks in Conservation First
stories.summary: Chester Zoo successfully bred secretarybirds for the first time in its 95-year history, with five chicks hatching to parents John and Jolene. With fewer than 6,700 secretarybirds left in the wild, the hatching is a major boost for the European breeding program, which produced only three other chicks elsewhere this year.

stories.headline: Ospreys Are Recovering in Britain Thanks to 'Pioneering Pairs' That Nest Far From Home
stories.summary: Researchers found that osprey recovery in Britain is being accelerated by independent-minded pairs that nest far from established populations, colonizing new territory rather than crowding existing sites. Conservationists are now using translocation and artificial nests to deliberately replicate this natural strategy and speed up the species' comeback.

stories.headline: 236-Million-Year-Old Fossil Suggests Mammal Ancestors Gave Birth to Live Young Far Earlier Than Thought
stories.summary: Paleontologists studying a cynodont fossil found a neonatal growth line and a newborn body size that match live-birth patterns seen in modern mammals rather than egg-layers, pushing back the known origin of live birth by roughly 95 million years. The find reshapes the story of how mammalian reproduction evolved.

stories.headline: Virginia Tech Security Guard Has Become a Local Celebrity for His Handmade Mini Rhino Trophies
stories.summary: Bryan Newton, a security guard at Virginia Tech's performing arts center, 3D-prints a custom themed mini rhino statue for every event as a prize in a staff guessing game, from a warrior rhino for a wrestling match to one in a witch hat for Halloween. The tradition has become a beloved keepsake that patrons and coworkers now look forward to collecting.

stories.headline: Fishing Guide's 911 Call Leads to Rescue of Entangled Manatee as Her Calf Watches
stories.summary: A fishing guide near St. Simons Island, Georgia, spotted an adult female manatee wrapped tightly in crab-trap line and called for help, triggering a two-day, multi-state response by Georgia DNR, Florida wildlife officials and the US Fish and Wildlife Service. The team freed her completely, fitted her with a satellite tag, and left her free to keep raising the dependent calf that stayed by her side throughout.

stories.headline: Scientists Discover Adult Brains Can Rebuild Their Own Damaged Support Cells
stories.summary: University of Zurich researchers found that astrocytes, brain support cells long thought unable to regenerate in adults, can send newly formed nuclei gliding across their extensions to repopulate tissue after injury. The discovery overturns a long-held assumption and points to new therapeutic targets for repairing brain damage and treating autoimmune neurological diseases.

stories.headline: Great Barrier Reef Gets a Reprieve as Monsoon Rains Cool the Water
stories.summary: A late monsoon season increased cloud cover and lowered sea temperatures this year, sparing the Great Barrier Reef the mass bleaching it suffered in 2024 and 2025. The Australian Institute of Marine Science's annual survey found coral cover actually rose 16.7% in the Northern Region and 10.2% in the Central Region, with 106 of 121 surveyed reefs showing moderate to high coral coverage.

stories.headline: Women's Professional Baseball Returns to the Field for the First Time Since 1954
stories.summary: The new Women's Professional Baseball League played its inaugural game in Springfield, Illinois, with 99-year-old Maybelle Blair — a veteran of the original All-American Girls Professional Baseball League — throwing out the first pitch despite recently broken ribs. The LA Queens beat the NY Heights to open a 30-game season, marking the first pro women's baseball competition in the US since the league that inspired 'A League of Their Own' folded in 1954.

stories.headline: Brown Student Spends Summer Helping Providence Teens Find Their Voice in English
stories.summary: Rising sophomore Justin Dunn spent four weeks teaching an English class for teens at the Providence Public Library through Brown University's SPRINT-iProv fellowship, taking students to a local market and having them build resumes so language skills stuck outside the classroom. Some of the library staff he worked alongside are immigrants who once learned English through the same program before returning to teach it themselves.

stories.headline: Rare 'Death Bloom' Agave Forces Botanical Garden to Cut Open Its Greenhouse Roof
stories.summary: A decade-old Agave sisalana at Birmingham Botanical Gardens in England has entered its once-in-a-lifetime 'death bloom,' with its flower spike growing so tall — over 18 feet — that horticulturists had to remove glasshouse ceiling panels to let it keep growing. The monocarpic plant is now producing hundreds of bulbils and seeds, plus four cloned 'pups,' to ensure new agaves carry on its genetic line after it dies.

stories.headline: Star Cluster Discovery Could Change How Scientists Measure the Universe
stories.summary: University of Missouri researchers found that the ratio of large to small stars varies depending on the environment where they form, challenging the long-held assumption that stars form in uniform proportions everywhere. The finding could improve how astronomers estimate galaxy mass and age, and may explain why some galaxies observed by the James Webb Space Telescope have looked more massive than expected.

stories.headline: Dogs' Brains Can Tell the Difference Between Fear and Sadness, Study Finds
stories.summary: Using brain scans, researchers from the University of Vienna, UNAM and Eotvos Lorand University found that dogs' brains respond differently to human faces showing fear versus sadness, the first evidence that dogs distinguish between specific negative emotions rather than just reading 'good' or 'bad.' Happy human faces lit up reward-related regions in the dogs' brains, hinting at just how finely tuned dogs are to their owners' feelings.

stories.headline: India Crosses 300 Gigawatts of Clean Power Capacity, Reaching 60% of Its 2030 Target
stories.summary: India's non-fossil fuel electricity capacity passed 300 GW as of July 31, 2026, now more than 54% of the country's total generation capacity. Solar power alone has grown from 2.8 GW in 2014 to nearly 165 GW today, putting the country past 60% of its goal to reach 500 GW of clean capacity by 2030.

stories.headline: Toddlers With Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy Show Rapid Motor Gains in New Drug Trial
stories.summary: In a Phase II trial, Binghamton University researchers gave the steroid-alternative drug vamorolone to boys aged 2 to under 4 with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. After just 12 weeks, gross-motor scores rose sharply with no serious side effects, raising hope that treatment can start before symptoms fully set in now that DMD has been added to newborn screening recommendations.

stories.headline: Team USA Smashes World U20 Record in Men's 4x100m Relay
stories.summary: At the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, the American quartet of Blake Hamilton, Dillon Mitchell, Kyler Brown and Tate Taylor ran 38.16 seconds to break the U20 world record in the men's 4x100m relay, beating the previous mark by more than a third of a second. Anchor Tate Taylor capped the meet with three gold medals.

stories.headline: Blind Dressage Horse Wins Competitions Using 'Equine Braille'
stories.summary: Milo, a 15-year-old Appaloosa who lost his sight to an eye condition, continues to compete successfully in dressage with rider Megan Share. The pair developed a tactile system of pressure cues so Milo can navigate the arena purely by feel, and he's now won the Royal Windsor Horse Show for the eighth year running.
